explain.text:
Per cent means out of every hundred, so 15% is 15 out of 100.[^1] As a fraction that is 15/100, and as a decimal 0.15, because a percentage turns into a decimal when you divide it by 100. 100% is the whole amount, and a percentage can go past it, so 150% is the whole and half as much again, which is 1.5 as a decimal.

To find a percentage of an amount, picture a bar for the whole, 100%, with the amount lined up underneath. 10% is a tenth, so 10% of 230 V is 230 ÷ 10 = 23 V, and 1% is a hundredth, 2.3 V. For any other percentage, change it to a decimal and multiply the amount by it, so 15% of 230 V is 230 × 0.15 = 34.5 V.[^2] The slips to watch are dividing by 10 instead of 100, which reads 3% as 0.3, and dividing by the percentage itself, which finds 20% by dividing by 20.[^3]

**A percentage is a number of hundredths, so divide it by 100 for its decimal and times the amount by that, as in 15% of 230 V = 230 × 0.15 = 34.5 V.**

practice.text:
**Rule of thumb:** Divide the percentage by 100 to get its decimal, then times the amount by it.[^2] 10% is a tenth and 1% is a hundredth, which makes a quick check.

**Worked example:** 7.5% of £80. As a decimal, 7.5 ÷ 100 = 0.075, and 80 × 0.075 = 6, so it is £6. As a check, 10% of £80 is £8, and 7.5% is a bit less.

**Common mistakes**
- Dividing by 10 instead of 100. 3% is 0.03, not 0.3, so 3% of 230 V is 6.9 V, not 69 V.[^3]
- Dividing by the percentage. Dividing £40 by 20 gives £2, a twentieth, which is only 5%. 20% of £40 is two tenths, £4 + £4 = £8.
- Taking only the part past 100%. 125% of 80 m is all 80 m and 25% more, so 100 m, not 20 m.

interactive.html:
A hundred squares, then a percentage bar with the amount underneath.

A percentage counts hundredths of the whole. The amounts are example values.
interactive.title: What a percentage is
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a percentage lining up with its amount on the percentage bar, 10% a tenth of the whole and 1% a hundredth, with the amount moving in step when you drag the marker, so 15% of 230 V is 230 × 0.15 = 34.5 V.

checks.label: The sign % stands for per cent, which means out of 100, so 15% is drawn as 15 of the grid's 100 squares and 3% as 3 of them (none before the answer)

To change a percentage to a decimal, divide by 100: 15% = 0.15, 3% = 0.03, 45% = 0.45, 35% = 0.35, 7.5% = 0.075, 125% = 1.25, 150% = 1.5, and every working that times by a decimal, in the five puzzles and the two demonstrations, uses its percentage divided by 100 and is true

The decimal multiplier method converts the percentage to a decimal and multiplies the amount by it: 15% of 230 V = 230 × 0.15 = 34.5 V, 20% of £40 = £8, 3% of 230 V = 6.9 V, 45% of 90 m = 40.5 m, 150% of 40 A = 60 A, 125% of 80 m = 100 m, 25% of 48 A = 12 A, 35% of £240 = £84, 7.5% of £80 = £6; each puzzle's working is true and gives its answer

Each puzzle accepts only its own answer, and every wrong answer offered is the one a named slip gives: dividing by 10 instead of 100 (3% as 0.3), dividing by the percentage (20% by dividing by 20), the percentage as it stands, or only the part past 100%
The drag puzzle takes 40.5 m only with the marker on 45% (from 80%, the hint says drag it left; from below, right), and the marker snaps to 5% steps from 0 to 100%

The bar lines the two scales up: the marker sits a share p/top of the way along, so 100% is the whole bar (two thirds of it on a bar that runs to 150%, four fifths on one to 125%), and the amount under every whole percentage from 0 to 100 is that many hundredths of 230 V

Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion within 2.5 s; shaded squares and parts start at least 0.2 s apart
The right answer is not always in the same place: across the eight puzzles it sits first, second and third at least twice each, and never three times running in one place

Nothing pops in or out: painted every 1/60 s through each demonstration and each right answer's motion (from the picture before Check to the finished one), no word or line changes its opacity by more than 0.5 from one frame to the next, nor do the whole's end labels as a marker is moved 1% at a time from 0 to 100%

notes.problem: Every entry in numbers has kind "constant", but 230 V, £40, 90 m, 40 A, 80 m, 48 A, £240 and £80 are example amounts chosen for the method (assumed, as ignores says) and each answer is computed from the shown rule; none is a fixed real-world value.

The lesson was written with no research.json, so it cites nothing, though the course's research notes hold publisher quotes for both slips it teaches (Oak: 3% read as 0.3; NCETM: "to find 20%, you must divide by 20") and for the decimal multiplier method (BBC Bitesize).
